title: Assignment EPPS 6355 - Grammar of Graphics
text:
Google Flu Trends (GFT) sought to detect surges of flu about one to two weeks brefore CDC, based on searches associated with this disease. The model in the beginning followed the CDC data very closely and was very successful. However, the expectation of continuously representing the data with accuracy never became real. GFT did not detect the 2009 H1N1 pandemic and overstimaed the incidence of flu by more than 199 weeds, and predicted more than double the medical appointments recorded by CDC for the 2012-2 seasons.
The failure is supposed to be due to a few factors. The “big data rubris” is the false presumption that big data can ultimately replace traditional monitoring. Google searches may reflect the concern of users regarding the sickness but not the sickness itself. Also, Google keeps changing its algorithms continuously, which must have caused relevant change to the way data is collected and classified. Also, one of the major problmes is that Google was not transparent and never published the terms it used for prediction, making it harder for researchers to validate the consistency of the method.
One example based on my own professional background as a former public sector auditor, is that our whitleblower line received a massive number of manifestations everyday, but most of them were not useful for auditing and fraud detection since most of the files were just citizens complaining about the government or services providade, never giving any useful information on whether there was some kind of fraud, where it was happening, who performed it etc. We had big data, but the data and its collection procedures were not designed to model the data according to our analytical needs.




In my understanding, overfitting occurs whenever a model learns not only the pattern but also the noice of the data in the training dataset. It is good to describe the current data, but bad to predict new ones. Overparametrization is when the model has so many tentative parameters that almost any series can be explained. GFT shows both concepts. With so many parameters, some terms will inevitably correlate with flu by chance. The model ends up trying to explain even what should not be explained.




The lecture titled Data Visualization and data Science, by Hadley Wickham, discussed the importance of visualizing data in any modern data workflow. Wickham addresses the data analysis cycle (loading data, cleansing data, transofrming, visualizing, modeling and reporting) and emphasizes that data viz should not only be used for final reporting but it is a crucial stage for exploratory analysis itself. It allows for the user to find patterns and anomalies, and to see the strucuture of the data that can not be seen from tabular data. Ascombe’s quartet is a classic example of it.
He also discussed the importance of the availability of tools such as R and the Tidyverse and Ggplot2 libraries, that are efficient and easy to implement, which relieves the cognitive toll on analysts, allowing for closer focus on problem resolution instead of worrying about handlingthe software and other implementations issues.

title: Assignment 03 - EPPS 6302
text:
library(tidycensus) 
library(tigris) 
library(sf) 
library(dplyr) 
library(ggplot2) 
library(readr) 
library(tidyr) 
options(tigris_use_cache = TRUE)





Run this only once IN THE CONSOLE DO NOT ADD API KEY TO THE SCRIPT

census_api_key("YOUR API KEY HERE", install = TRUE, overwrite = TRUE)

ATTENTION! API KEYS expires quickly. Request a new one whenever needed.




Download a complete list of codes and descriptions available for the 2024 ACS 5-year (“acs5”) and stores it in a table called vars. It is like a data dictionary
The Census Bureau has thousands of variables in the ACS, and each one is identified by a cryptic code like B19013_001 or B17001_002 — nobody memorizes these. load_variables() downloads the full catalog of available variable codes and their human-readable descriptions (like a dictionary or index) and stores it in vars.
This step doesn’t download any actual data about counties, states, income, or poverty numbers. It’s purely a reference table you browse through (you filtered it with grepl(“^B19”, name)) to figure out which exact codes correspond to the concepts you want to study — in your case, median household income and poverty. You use this step once, just to look things up, then you already know the codes you need (B19013_001, B17001_002, B17001_001), which get hardcoded into my_vars in the next part of the script.

vars <- load_variables(2023, "acs5")

Keeps only the rows where the variable name starts with “B19”.

grepl is a text/pattern search (regex), and \^B19 means “starts with B19”.

Variables starting with B19 are all income-related, so this filters the giant dictionary down to just the income variables.

slice_head can also capture the top n rows of each group with group_by()


vars <- dplyr::filter(vars, grepl("^B19", name)) %>% 
  dplyr::slice_head(n = 10) 
print(vars)

 9 B19001A_009 Estimate!!Total:!!$40,000 to $44,999 Household Income … tract    
10 B19001A_010 Estimate!!Total:!!$45,000 to $49,999 Household Income … tract    





Now that you know exactly which variable codes you want, get_acs() is the function that actually contacts the Census API and pulls the real numbers for those specific codes, for the specific geography you chose (here, counties in Missouri). This is the step that returns actual estimates and margins of error for real places, plus (because geometry = TRUE) the map boundaries for each county.
But before, let’s set up the paramers for our search.

survey <- "acs5" 
year_acs <- 2024 
state_abbr <- "MO" 
geo_level <- "county" 
my_vars <- c( 
  income = "B19013_001", # median household income 
  pov = "B17001_002", # people below poverty 
  povden = "B17001_001" # poverty universe = denominator 
  )




Let’s now download the data

acs_wide <- get_acs( 
  geography = geo_level, 
  variables = my_vars, 
  state = state_abbr, 
  year = year_acs, 
  survey = survey, 
  geometry = TRUE, 
  # 'wide' for variables in columns 'long' is default for variables in rows 
  output = "wide" 
  )

In R, an object can be more than one thing at the same time:

data.frame means it’s a table
sf means it’s also a spatial object (simple features) because it has a special column storing the geometry
That extra layer is what lets you use geom_sf() in ggplot() to draw maps


class(acs_wide)

[1] "sf"         "data.frame"





The chunk below calculates the poverty rate for each county: it takes the estimated number of people below the poverty line (povE, from B17001_002) and divides it by the total population in the “poverty universe” for that county (povdenE, from B17001_001 — the denominator, i.e., the population this poverty measure applies to). The result is a proportion (for example, 0.15 = 15% of people in that county are below the poverty line).
When you simply divide two numbers that each already have their own margins of error (povM and povdenM), you can’t just divide the margins of error too (povM / povdenM would be wrong). Because povE (people in poverty) is a subset of povdenE (everyone), the two estimates are statistically correlated, and there’s a specific Census Bureau formula for correctly calculating the margin of error of a proportion derived from two other estimates.
moe_prop() is a function from the tidycensus package itself that already implements that official Census formula for you. It takes: - povE — numerator estimate (people in poverty) - povdenE — denominator estimate (total population) - povM — numerator’s MOE - povdenM — denominator’s MOE
And returns the correct MOE for the pov_rate you just calculated.
In practice: without this line, you’d have each county’s poverty rate but no idea how reliable that number is. With pov_moe, you can say, for example, “this county’s poverty rate is 15% ± 3 percentage points” — which is essential for the part of the assignment that asks you to compare areas and check whether their confidence intervals overlap (the “Uncertainty check” deliverable).

acs_wide <- acs_wide %>% 
  mutate(
    pov_rate = povE / povdenE, 
    pov_moe = moe_prop(povE, povdenE, povM, povdenM)
    )





ggplot(acs_wide) + 
geom_sf(aes(fill = incomeE), color = NA) + 
  scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "Median HH Income") + 
  labs(title = paste0("ACS ", 
                      year_acs, 
                      " 5-year: Median Income — ", 
                      state_abbr, 
                      " (", 
                      geo_level, 
                      ")"
                      ), 
       caption = "Source: U.S. Census Bureau via tidycensus") + 
  theme_minimal() + 
  theme(#text = element_text(family = "Palatino"),
        plot.title = element_text(size = 14, face = "bold"),

title: Assignment 1 - EPPS 6356
text:
In his paper (1973), Anscombe claims that visualizing data is crucial for statistical analysis. To support his claim, he presented a dataset that generated four different visualizations in which the data displays totally different behaviors, even though the regression summary was exactly the same for all. That illustrates the fact that only by running statistical/mathematical metrics may not be enough for a scientist to understand the underlying nature of data.
In his paper, Anscombe suggested that data that is not linear could be adjusted by applying transformation functions to the x-axis, to the y-axis or both. Today, with libraries such as the scikit-learn library in Python, it is possible to conduct multiple types of transformations not only to linearize data but also to shape the data under several desired statistical distributions.
Thus, using Python is a possible and efficient method I would suggest to go around problems associated with nonlinear data, as addressed by Anscombe.

## Anscombe (1973) Quartlet
data(anscombe)  # Load Anscombe's data
View(anscombe) # View the data
summary(anscombe)

angle=22.5

status=data.frame(x=numeric(0), y=numeric(0), alfa=numeric(0))
points=data.frame(x1 = 0, y1 = 0, x2 = NA, y2 = NA, alfa=90, depth=1)


# Generating data
# Note: may take a minute or two

for (action in actions)
{
  if (action=="F")
  {
    x=points[1, "x1"]+cos(points[1, "alfa"]*(pi/180))
    y=points[1, "y1"]+sin(points[1, "alfa"]*(pi/180))
    points[1,"x2"]=x
    points[1,"y2"]=y
    data.frame(x1 = x, y1 = y, x2 = NA, y2 = NA,
               alfa=points[1, "alfa"],
               depth=points[1,"depth"]) %>% rbind(points)->points
  }
  if (action %in% c("+", "-")){
    alfa=points[1, "alfa"]
    points[1, "alfa"]=eval(parse(text=paste0("alfa",action, angle)))
  }
  if(action=="["){
    data.frame(x=points[1, "x1"], y=points[1, "y1"], alfa=points[1, "alfa"]) %>%
      rbind(status) -> status
    points[1, "depth"]=points[1, "depth"]+1
  }

               alfa=status[1, "alfa"],
               depth=depth-1) %>%
      rbind(points) -> points
    status[-1,]->status
  }
}

In his paper (1973), Anscombe claims that visualizing data is crucial for statistical analysis. To support his claim, he presented a dataset that generated four different visualizations in which the data displays totally different behaviors, even though the regression summary was exactly the same for all. That illustrates the fact that only by running statistical/mathematical metrics may not be enough for a scientist to understand the underlying nature of data.
In his paper, Anscombe suggested that data that is not linear could be adjusted by applying transformation functions to the x-axis, to the y-axis or both. Today, with libraries such as the scikit-learn library in Python, it is possible to conduct multiple types of transformations not only to linearize data but also to shape the data under several desired statistical distributions.
Thus, using Python is a possible and efficient method I would suggest to go around problems associated with nonlinear data, as addressed by Anscombe.

That reveals that without visualizing the data, an analyst could make serious modeling mistakes. Plotting the data, however reveals that each data set behaves very differently from the others. Data set 2 and data set 4, for example, are clearly nonlinear, which is prohibitive for regressions.

Another way to see the regressions is using confidence intervals. Once again, a different visualization proves that the data sets are different, regardless of the equivalent metrics:

library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)

data(anscombe)

plot_anscombe <- function(dataset_num) {
  x_col <- paste0("x", dataset_num)
  y_col <- paste0("y", dataset_num)
  formula <- as.formula(paste(y_col, "~", x_col))
  mod <- lm(formula, data = anscombe)
  intercept <- round(coef(mod)[1], 3)
  slope     <- round(coef(mod)[2], 3)
  r2        <- round(summary(mod)$r.squared, 3)
  rse       <- round(summary(mod)$sigma, 3)
  stats_label <- paste0(
    "Intercept = ", intercept, "\n",
    "Slope = ", slope, "\n",
    "R² = ", r2, "\n",
    "RSE = ", rse
  )
  
  # Building confidence bands
  ggplot(anscombe, aes_string(x = x_col, y = y_col)) +
    geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = TRUE, 
                color = "blue", fill = "lightblue", alpha = 0.4) +
    geom_point(fill = "tomato", color = "red", shape = 21, size = 3) +
    annotate("text", x = 3.5, y = 11.5, label = stats_label, 
             hjust = 0, size = 3.2, family = "sans") +
    scale_x_continuous(limits = c(3, 19)) +
    scale_y_continuous(limits = c(3, 13)) +
    labs(title = paste("Dataset", dataset_num), x = paste0("x", dataset_num), y = paste0("y", dataset_num)) +
    theme_bw()
}

Another way to see the regressions is using confidence intervals. Once again, a different visualization proves that the data sets are different, regardless of the equivalent metrics:

library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)

data(anscombe)

plot_anscombe <- function(dataset_num) {
  x_col <- paste0("x", dataset_num)
  y_col <- paste0("y", dataset_num)
  formula <- as.formula(paste(y_col, "~", x_col))
  mod <- lm(formula, data = anscombe)
  intercept <- round(coef(mod)[1], 3)
  slope     <- round(coef(mod)[2], 3)
  r2        <- round(summary(mod)$r.squared, 3)
  rse       <- round(summary(mod)$sigma, 3)
  stats_label <- paste0(
    "Intercept = ", intercept, "\n",
    "Slope = ", slope, "\n",
    "R² = ", r2, "\n",
    "RSE = ", rse
  )
  
  # Building confidence bands
  ggplot(anscombe, aes_string(x = x_col, y = y_col)) +
    geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = TRUE, 
                color = "blue", fill = "lightblue", alpha = 0.4) +
    geom_point(fill = "tomato", color = "red", shape = 21, size = 3) +
    annotate("text", x = 3.5, y = 11.5, label = stats_label, 
             hjust = 0, size = 3.2, family = "sans") +
    scale_x_continuous(limits = c(3, 19)) +
    scale_y_continuous(limits = c(3, 13)) +
    labs(title = paste("Dataset", dataset_num), x = paste0("x", dataset_num), y = paste0("y", dataset_num)) +
    theme_bw()
}

Scraping is a great tool when the data are publicly visible but are not available via API for mass download. Here it was the wrong choice because the World Bank had a better documented and API-available source.

title: Research
text:
Machine Learning applied to Public Sector Auditing: A case study with data from the department of health of the state of São Paulo, Brazil

Abstract:
Machine Learning (ML), as a field of Artificial Intelligence (AI), has become increasingly popular due to its ease of learning, scalability, and low cost. Both industry and academia have researched useful and feasible ways to apply ML algorithms for practical use in multiple fields, both academic and professional, taking advantage of their ability to learn patterns to predict future variables, classify or group data, and detect anomalous observations. Although the private sector has quickly evolved in studying the application of ML to financial fraud, stock market modeling and financial distress prediction, the application of these techniques in the public sector, namely in public audit, still demands further research for practical use. In this paper, I conduct a review of the current literature on machine learning applications for management-related fields and propose a case study to advance its application to public audit. I identified the Isolation Forest (iForest) algorithm as one of the most effective, scalable, and recognized for detecting anomalies. I applied it to a dataset with expenditure data from the Department of Health of the city of São Paulo, Brazil, and found that the algorithm can be of practical use for anomalous transaction value detection, but ineffective in identifying expenditure misclassification. The paper contributes to the scarce literature on the application of ML to public audit and seeks to promote further investigation for public oversight and improved management.
